content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Hell' primarily denotes the final state or place of divine punishment for the unrepentant wicked after death and final judgment — classically understood as eternal, conscious separation from God accompanied by torment, frequently symbolized by unquenchable fire, darkness, and 'weeping and gnashing of teeth.' In this dominant (traditionalist) reading, the fire and worm imagery symbolizes real, everlasting retributive punishment and exclusion from God's presence, contrasted with the eternal life of the redeemed.", "primary_basis": ["Matthew 25:41, 46 (eternal fire prepared for the devil; eternal punishment vs. eternal life)", "Mark 9:43-48 (Gehenna, where 'their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched,' echoing Isaiah 66:24)", "Matthew 10:28 (fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna)", "Matthew 5:22, 29-30 (danger of the fire of Gehenna)", "Luke 16:19-31 (the rich man in torment in Hades)", "Revelation 20:10-15 (the lake of fire; the second death)", "Revelation 14:10-11 (the smoke of their torment rises forever)", "2 Thessalonians 1:9 (eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord)", "Matthew 13:41-42, 49-50 (furnace of fire; weeping and gnashing of teeth)", "Jude 7 (punishment of eternal fire)", "Daniel 12:2 (everlasting contempt)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Eternal conscious torment understood metaphorically rather than as literal flames: the fire, darkness, and worm are symbols of the anguish of final separation from God, not physical descriptions. Held by many traditionalists (e.g., Calvin, many evangelicals, C.S. Lewis's 'doors locked from the inside' framing of hell as self-chosen separation).", "basis": ["Matthew 8:12 and 22:13 (outer darkness — held to be incompatible with literal fire, indicating symbolism)", "2 Thessalonians 1:9 (separation from the presence of the Lord)", "Revelation 20:14 (death and Hades thrown into the fire — abstractions, suggesting symbol)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Annihilationism / conditional immortality: hell's fire consumes and finally destroys the wicked, ending their existence; 'eternal punishment' means a punishment with everlasting effect (destruction), not everlasting conscious suffering. Advocated by Seventh-day Adventists and a notable evangelical minority (e.g., John Stott, Edward Fudge).", "basis": ["Matthew 10:28 (destroy both soul and body)", "2 Thessalonians 1:9 (eternal destruction)", "John 3:16 (perish vs. eternal life)", "Malachi 4:1-3 (the wicked burned to ashes)", "Romans 6:23 (the wages of sin is death)", "Revelation 20:14 (the second death)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Universal reconciliation (apokatastasis): hell is real but remedial and temporary; ultimately all will be reconciled to God. Associated with Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, and modern advocates (e.g., David Bentley Hart); hopeful-universalist variants appear in some Catholic and Orthodox thought (e.g., von Balthasar).", "basis": ["1 Corinthians 15:22, 28 (in Christ all made alive; God all in all)", "Colossians 1:19-20 (reconciling all things)", "Philippians 2:10-11 (every knee shall bow)", "1 Timothy 2:4 (God desires all to be saved)", "Romans 5:18 and 11:32 (justification/mercy for all)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Lexical/scholarly distinction reading: 'hell' in English conflates distinct biblical terms — Sheol/Hades (the grave or intermediate realm of the dead), Gehenna (final judgment, named for the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem), and Tartarus (2 Peter 2:4). On this reading many 'hell' passages refer to death or an intermediate state, not final punishment. This distinction is standard in academic biblical studies and modern translations.", "basis": ["Psalm 16:10 and Acts 2:27, 31 (Sheol/Hades as realm of the dead)", "Revelation 20:13-14 (Hades distinguished from and destroyed in the lake of fire)", "Jeremiah 7:31-32 and 19:6 (Valley of Hinnom background to Gehenna)", "2 Peter 2:4 (Tartarus)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Historicized/this-worldly reading: Jesus' Gehenna warnings refer primarily to imminent temporal judgment on Jerusalem (e.g., AD 70) or national catastrophe, using prophetic hyperbole, rather than mapping directly onto a doctrine of postmortem torment (associated with some strands of N.T. Wright's work and preterist interpretation).", "basis": ["Jeremiah 7:30-34 and 19:1-15 (Hinnom as image of national judgment)", "Matthew 23:33-38 and 24:1-2 (judgment coming on that generation and the temple)", "Luke 13:1-5 (warnings of temporal perishing)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Roman Catholic framework distinguishing hell (definitive self-exclusion from communion with God, chief punishment being eternal separation) from purgatory (temporary purification of the saved) and the harrowing of hell (Christ's descent to the dead). Hell proper remains eternal separation; the fire imagery is often treated as expressing that reality.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:41, 46", "1 Corinthians 3:12-15 (used for purgatorial purification, distinct from hell)", "1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 with the Apostles' Creed clause 'he descended into hell' (Christ's descent to the dead/Hades)"], "prominence": "common"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a recognizable, historically dominant consensus that 'hell' signifies final divine judgment and punishment of the unredeemed, expressed through fire/Gehenna imagery. However, the term is unusually contested on secondary questions: (a) literal vs. metaphorical fire, (b) eternal conscious torment vs. annihilation vs. eventual universal reconciliation, and (c) the conflation in older English translations of Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, and Tartarus under one word 'hell,' which modern scholarship and most modern translations now distinguish. The core consensus (postmortem judgment and exclusion from God) is settled across Catholic, Orthodox, and most Protestant traditions; the precise nature and duration of that state is the main locus of ongoing debate."}
